eras.title: Brooklyn to Columbia
eras.summary: The son of immigrants from Carpathian Ruthenia, Friedman grew up above a dry-goods shop in Rahway, New Jersey, won a scholarship to Rutgers, discovered economics in the depths of the Depression, met Rose Director at Chicago, and spent the war years as a Treasury tax economist and a wartime statistician.

eras.title: The Chicago Years
eras.summary: Three decades on the faculty of the University of Chicago produced the permanent income hypothesis, the Monetary History, Capitalism and Freedom, the natural rate of unemployment, the Newsweek column, the campaign against the draft and the counter-revolution against Keynes that became known as monetarism.

eras.title: Nobel and Free to Choose
eras.summary: The 1976 Nobel Prize, retirement from Chicago to the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the PBS series and book Free to Choose, made with Rose, which carried his ideas to a mass audience at the moment Thatcher and Reagan were taking office.

eras.title: Public Intellectual
eras.summary: Adviser to President Reagan, recipient of the Presidential Medal of Freedom and the National Medal of Science, author of Money Mischief and the memoir Two Lucky People, founder with Rose of a school-choice foundation, and still writing on money the week he died.

eras.title: Legacy
eras.summary: Rose's death, the institute at Chicago that bears his name, Friedman Legacy Day each 31 July, a central bank consensus built on his critique of the 1930s, and continuing argument over the ideas he spent a lifetime defending.

events.title: Born in Brooklyn
events.text: Milton Friedman is born to Sarah Ethel Landau and Jenő Saul Friedman, Jewish immigrants from Beregszász in Carpathian Ruthenia, then part of Austria-Hungary. He is the fourth child and only son. The family soon moves to Rahway, New Jersey, where his parents run a small dry-goods store.

events.title: Graduates from Rahway High School
events.text: Friedman finishes high school shortly before his sixteenth birthday, in the year his father dies. A state scholarship takes him to Rutgers University, where he expects to become an actuary and waits tables and clerks to pay his way.

events.title: B.A. from Rutgers University
events.text: Two young instructors, Arthur Burns and Homer Jones, turn him from mathematics towards economics. With the country in the third year of the Depression, he decides the pressing problem of the age is economic. He wins scholarships to both Brown (for mathematics) and Chicago (for economics), and chooses Chicago.

events.title: M.A. from the University of Chicago
events.text: In Jacob Viner's price theory class the students are seated alphabetically. Friedman finds himself next to Rose Director, a fellow graduate student from Portland, Oregon. He studies under Viner, Frank Knight and Henry Simons, and takes the Chicago approach to economics as a way of seeing the world.

events.title: A year of statistics at Columbia
events.text: A fellowship takes him to Columbia University, where Harold Hotelling teaches him mathematical statistics and Wesley Mitchell introduces him to the empirical, institutional study of business cycles. He returns to Chicago as research assistant to Henry Schultz, then working on the statistical theory of demand.

events.title: New Deal Washington
events.text: Unable to find an academic post, Friedman joins the National Resources Committee to work on a large study of consumer budgets. The data on how families spend their income will later feed his theory of the consumption function. He later said the New Deal jobs were a lifesaver for young economists of his generation.

events.title: National Bureau of Economic Research
events.text: He joins the NBER staff to assist Simon Kuznets on a study of professional incomes. Their finding that the medical profession restricted entry and raised doctors' fees provokes a dispute within the Bureau that delays publication of the book, Income from Independent Professional Practice, until 1945.

events.title: Marries Rose Director
events.text: Milton and Rose marry six years after meeting in Viner's class. Rose, an economist in her own right and sister of the Chicago law professor Aaron Director, becomes his closest collaborator and co-author of the books that reach the widest public. Their daughter Janet is born in 1943 and son David in 1945.

events.title: Visiting professor at Wisconsin
events.text: A year at the University of Wisconsin ends without a permanent post after a departmental fight in which antisemitism played a part. Friedman returns east.

events.title: Treasury tax economist
events.text: At the Treasury's Division of Tax Research he works on wartime tax policy and helps design income-tax withholding at source, the system the United States still uses. He later called it a necessary wartime measure that he wished had been abolished when the war ended.

events.title: Statistical Research Group
events.text: As associate director of the Statistical Research Group he works alongside Abraham Wald, Harold Hotelling and W. Allen Wallis on wartime problems, from the design of proximity fuzes to sampling inspection. The group's work on sequential analysis is one of the war's lasting contributions to statistics.

events.title: Minnesota, and Roofs or Ceilings?
events.text: A year as associate professor at the University of Minnesota, sharing an office with George Stigler. Together they write Roofs or Ceilings?, a pamphlet against rent control, published by the Foundation for Economic Education in 1946. It is his first piece of public advocacy.

events.title: Ph.D. from Columbia University
events.text: The professional-incomes study with Kuznets, finally published, serves as his doctoral dissertation. That autumn the University of Chicago offers him the post left vacant by Jacob Viner. He accepts, and stays for thirty years.

events.title: Joins the Chicago faculty
events.text: Friedman arrives as associate professor of economics, becoming full professor in 1948. He takes over the Money and Banking Workshop, a seminar whose rigorous argument and empirical testing shape a generation of students, including future Nobel laureates and the Chilean economists later known as the Chicago Boys.

events.title: Founding of the Mont Pelerin Society
events.text: At Friedrich Hayek's invitation he attends the ten-day meeting that founds the Mont Pelerin Society, an international circle of liberal scholars. He is one of the youngest present. He serves as the Society's president from 1970 to 1972.

events.title: Marshall Plan consultant in Paris
events.text: Advising the Economic Cooperation Administration on the Schuman Plan, he writes the memorandum that becomes The Case for Flexible Exchange Rates, arguing that floating currencies would serve Europe better than fixed parities. Two decades later the Bretton Woods system collapses and the world adopts his prescription.

events.title: John Bates Clark Medal
events.text: The AEA awards him its medal for the most distinguished American economist under forty.

events.title: Essays in Positive Economics
events.text: The collection opens with The Methodology of Positive Economics, which argues that a theory should be judged by the accuracy of its predictions rather than the realism of its assumptions. It becomes the most cited essay on economic method of the twentieth century.

events.title: A year at Cambridge
events.text: A Fulbright fellowship takes the family to England, where Friedman spends a year among the Keynesians of Cambridge. He later recalled that he was too right-wing for the economists and too left-wing for the college, and enjoyed himself enormously.

events.title: The Role of Government in Education
events.text: In an essay in a volume edited by Robert Solo he proposes that government fund schooling through vouchers parents could spend at any approved school, public or private. It is the origin of the modern school-choice movement.

events.title: The Quantity Theory of Money: A Restatement
events.place: Studies in the Quantity Theory of Money
events.text: His introduction to a volume of workshop papers recasts the quantity theory as a theory of the demand for money. It is the theoretical foundation of the monetarist counter-revolution.

events.title: The Wabash lectures
events.text: A series of lectures for the Volker Fund, transcribed and edited by Rose, becomes the manuscript of Capitalism and Freedom.

events.title: A Theory of the Consumption Function
events.text: Households, he argues, spend according to their expected long-run or permanent income, not their income this year. The permanent income hypothesis overturns the simple Keynesian consumption function and is the first of the two achievements cited by the Nobel committee.

events.title: A Program for Monetary Stability
events.text: From the Millar Lectures he sets out the case for a fixed rule: let the money supply grow at a steady, announced rate and let the central bank do nothing else. The k-percent rule becomes the signature policy proposal of monetarism.

events.title: Capitalism and Freedom
events.text: Written with Rose's assistance, the book argues that economic freedom is a precondition of political freedom and proposes floating exchange rates, school vouchers, a negative income tax, an end to occupational licensing and a volunteer army. Ignored by the major reviews at first, it goes on to sell more than half a million copies and is translated into eighteen languages.

events.title: A Monetary History of the United States, 1867–1960
events.place: Princeton University Press, for the NBER
events.text: With Anna Jacobson Schwartz he traces a century of money and shows that the Federal Reserve turned the recession of 1929 into the Great Depression by allowing the money stock to fall by a third. The chapter on the Great Contraction changes how central banks understand their job.

events.title: Inflation: Causes and Consequences
events.text: In a lecture published by the Council for Economic Education in Bombay he states the sentence most often quoted from him: inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon.

events.title: Adviser to Barry Goldwater
events.text: His first role in a presidential campaign. Goldwater loses in a landslide, but the relationship with the conservative movement brings Friedman a national platform.

events.title: The Newsweek column begins
events.text: Newsweek invites Friedman, Paul Samuelson and Henry Wallich to write a rotating column on economics. Friedman writes more than three hundred columns over eighteen years, bringing price theory and monetary economics to a weekly audience of millions.

events.title: The Role of Monetary Policy
events.text: In his presidential address to the AEA he argues that there is a natural rate of unemployment, that the trade-off between inflation and unemployment on the Phillips curve is temporary, and that attempts to push unemployment below the natural rate will produce ever-accelerating inflation. The stagflation of the 1970s makes the address look prophetic.

events.title: Adviser to Richard Nixon
events.text: He advises the Nixon campaign and, after the election, is an informal adviser to the President, though he breaks publicly with the administration over the wage and price controls of 1971.

events.title: The Gates Commission and the end of the draft
events.text: Appointed to the President's Commission on an All-Volunteer Armed Force, Friedman is its most forceful member. When General Westmoreland says he does not want to command an army of mercenaries, Friedman asks whether he would rather command an army of slaves. The commission reports unanimously for a volunteer force in 1970; conscription ends in 1973.

events.title: The Social Responsibility of Business Is to Increase Its Profits
events.text: The essay argues that corporate executives are the agents of shareholders and that spending company money on social causes is a form of taxation without representation. Known as the Friedman doctrine, it frames the debate about corporate purpose for the next half century.

events.title: Six days in Chile
events.text: On a visit arranged by a private foundation he lectures on inflation and meets General Pinochet for forty-five minutes, afterwards sending a letter urging a sharp cut in money growth and government spending. The visit brings protests that follow him for years, including at the Nobel ceremony. He said he gave the same advice to communist governments and that he never received a fee from Chile.

events.title: Nobel Prize announced
events.text: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awards him the Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel for his achievements in the fields of consumption analysis, monetary history and theory and for his demonstration of the complexity of stabilization policy. He hears the news in a Detroit parking garage, from reporters.

events.title: Nobel ceremony and lecture
events.text: A demonstrator interrupts the ceremony in protest at the Chile visit. Three days later Friedman delivers his Nobel lecture, Inflation and Unemployment, extending the natural-rate argument to explain why high inflation can coexist with high unemployment.

events.title: Retires from Chicago; joins the Hoover Institution
events.text: After thirty years, Milton and Rose leave Chicago for San Francisco. He becomes a Senior Research Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, where he remains for the rest of his life.

events.title: On Donahue
events.text: His appearances on Phil Donahue's daytime talk show, answering a studio audience on greed, welfare and capitalism, become some of the most watched economic arguments ever broadcast. Clips circulate for decades.

events.title: Free to Choose
events.text: The ten-part television series, filmed around the world from Hong Kong to the floor of the Chicago exchanges, airs on PBS from January 1980. Each episode pairs a documentary with a debate. The companion book, written with Rose, is the best-selling non-fiction book in the United States that year.

events.title: Adviser to Ronald Reagan
events.text: A member of Reagan's campaign economic advisory group, Friedman serves on the President's Economic Policy Advisory Board from 1981 to 1988.

events.title: Tyranny of the Status Quo
events.text: With Rose he examines why a new administration has only a few months to change the direction of government before the iron triangle of beneficiaries, bureaucrats and politicians reasserts itself. A three-part PBS series accompanies the book.

events.title: Presidential Medal of Freedom and National Medal of Science
events.text: President Reagan awards him the Presidential Medal of Freedom at a White House ceremony. The same year he receives the National Medal of Science, the country's highest scientific honour.

events.title: An Open Letter to Bill Bennett
events.text: To the newly appointed drug czar he argues that prohibition is the source of the violence and corruption of the drug trade, as it was of alcohol in the 1920s, and that drugs should be treated as a health problem rather than a crime. He had made the same case in Newsweek in 1972.

events.title: Free to Choose, 1990 edition
events.text: A five-part updated version of the series, filmed after the fall of the Berlin Wall and introduced by celebrity hosts including Arnold Schwarzenegger, revisits the arguments of 1980 in a changed world.

events.title: Money Mischief
events.text: Episodes in monetary history, from the stone money of Yap to the free-silver crusade of the 1890s and the inflations of the 1970s, written for the general reader.

events.title: The Milton and Rose D. Friedman Foundation
events.text: Milton and Rose establish a foundation to advance school choice, the policy he first proposed in 1955. It is now known as EdChoice.

events.title: Two Lucky People
events.text: Milton and Rose publish their joint memoir, written in alternating voices, covering sixty years of marriage, economics and argument.

events.title: Ninetieth birthday at Chicago
events.text: At a conference in his honour, Federal Reserve governor Ben Bernanke closes his remarks on the Great Depression: Regarding the Great Depression, you're right, we did it. We're very sorry. But thanks to you, we won't do it again.

events.title: A last long interview
events.text: At ninety-three he sits for an hour with Charlie Rose, reviewing his life, the Federal Reserve, Iraq, drugs, school choice and the euro, as sharp as ever.

events.title: Dies in San Francisco
events.text: Milton Friedman dies of heart failure at ninety-four. His final column, Why Money Matters, appears in The Wall Street Journal the next day, arguing once more that the quantity of money, not interest rates, is what the Federal Reserve should watch.

events.title: The Milton Friedman Institute
events.text: The University of Chicago announces a research institute in his name, over the objections of faculty who see it as an endorsement of his politics. In 2011 it is renamed the Becker Friedman Institute for Economics, honouring him together with Gary Becker.

events.title: Rose Friedman dies
events.text: Rose Director Friedman dies at ninety-eight, three years after Milton. Together they had written Free to Choose, Tyranny of the Status Quo and Two Lucky People, and founded the school-choice foundation that continues their work.

events.title: Centennial and Friedman Legacy Day
events.text: The centenary of his birth is marked by conferences at Chicago, Hoover and around the world. School-choice groups observe Friedman Legacy Day on his birthday each year.

events.title: Milton Friedman: The Last Conservative
events.text: Jennifer Burns of Stanford publishes the first full biography drawing on the Friedman papers at Hoover, restoring Rose Director, Anna Schwartz and Dorothy Brady to their places in the making of his ideas.
